On Tuesday, December 20, 2022 at 9:04:44 AM UTC-5 dan.gatti wrote:
>
> It depends on what you’re doing. If you want to map albino and agouti, you could create two binary phenotypes as you describe and map each one. You should get a peak on Chr 7 for albino and Chr 2 for agouti.
>
>
>
> If you’re doing QC to see if you have sample mixups, we use the albino and agouti loci. Find the marker closest to the ‘Tyr’ gene on Chr 7 and get the 36-state diplotypes (from maxmarg).  Then join those with your coat colors. Every row with ‘albino’ coat should have either ‘AA’, ‘AD’, or ‘DD’ diplotypes. And vice-versa.
>
>
>
> Find the marker closest to the ‘a’ gene on Chr 2 and get the 36-state diplotypes (from maxmarg).  Then join those with your coat colors. Every row with ‘black’ coat should have either ‘AA’, ‘AB’, or ‘B’ diplotypes. And vice-versa. However, albino masks black, so you may see some albino mice carrying the black allele and that’s OK.
>
>
>
> Dan
>
>
>
> From: rqtl2...@googlegroups.com <rqtl2...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of Mark Sfeir
> Sent: Friday, December 16, 2022 12:32 PM
> To: R/qtl2 discussion <rqtl2...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] LOD score consistency check with DO mice
>
>
>
> I understand that when doing QTL analysis using mice, calculating LOD scores by treating coat color as a phenotype and seeing whether known coat color QTL's show up in the results seems to be a meaningful check on calculation integrity. I'm looking for guidance on how to most effectively do this check.
>
>
>
> Currently we have coat colors for our DO mice encoded as a single covariate variable (including white, agouti, black, and tan qualitatively). My best idea for how to do this consistency check would be to pass the covariate data instead as phenotype data to scan1, but only after expanding the covariate data into 2 binary variables to represent all 4 possible coat colors. Using two binary variables, though, to encode the coat color information when checking this way would necessarily involve calculating two separate sets of LOD scores, which isn't as simple to present as a calculation integrity check as one LOD score curve would be.
>
>
>
> Would this be unnecessarily complicated compared to other approaches to this kind of check, or possibly a better informative way to do it in relation to coat color and all the QTL's that influence it? Maybe enough independent QTL's govern just these 4 coat colors that 2 binary variables would be needed to identify them in the results? Or maybe it would be sufficient to just use one binary variable to represent either black color vs any other color?
>
>
>
> -Mark Sfeir
>
> Research tech at UNC NRI

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Didn't converge error with binary model
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl2-disc] Didn't converge error with binary model
messages.body_plain:
I recently got the same warning when using scan1 with model="binary". Setting maxit as high as 10^7 didn't resolve the warning about convergence (and took a while), whereas decreasing the eta_max by trial and error to a value of 15 did.

When limiting the max value of the linear predictor eta_max in this way without a great understanding of the functional significance of that linear predictor in the calculations, I fear I may be producing low quality results. It would help me to get a pointer to some reference or otherwise have explained how adjusting the eta_max value affects scan1's calculations, and how dangerous it is to adjust eta_max too low in terms of quality of results.

Separately, adjusting the bintol as high as 10^-4 resolved at least one convergence warning in my case, but I'm not sure whether the bintol is more important than eta_max for the results.

I'd appreciate any input here,
Mark Sfeir
Research tech at UNC

On Monday, December 16, 2019 at 12:06:13 PM UTC-5 joanna...@gmail.com wrote:
> Great! Thanks for the help - adjusting the eta_max helps it converge better.
>
> On Sat, Dec 14, 2019 at 11:10 AM Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > It's a warning not an error. The binary scan fits a logistic regression at each locus, which uses an iterative algorithm which is apparently not converging in the chosen number of iterations. You can also try playing with the arguments 'bintol' (the tolerance for convergence, default 1e-6) and 'eta_max' (maximum value of linear predictor, default ~28).
> >
> > The dips in the LOD score likely correspond to positions where the algorithm is not converging.
> >
> > karl
> >
> > On 12/13/19 2:03 PM, Joanna R. wrote:
> > > Hi Karl,
> > >
> > > I'm get an error message running a binary scan in QTL2, and the output looks a little odd.
> > > 2: In scan_binary_onechr(genoprobs, pheno, addcovar, maxit, tol, qr_tol,  :
> > >   binreg didn't converge
> > > If I use the default model (obviously inappropriately, because it's a binary trait), I don't get quite such dramatic pits or the "didn't converge" error message (see below). Changing maxit doesn't seem to help.
> > >
> > >
> > > For a little more context: this is a map from a non-model system (Rumex) with very unevenly distributed recombination (mostly at the tips of chromosomes). This is simply a scan to confirm the identity of the sex chromosome by localizing sex as a phenotype; multiple other sources of data (e.g. GWAS from a population, distribution of XY polymorphisms in a pedigree cross, etc.) localize the sex-linked region to the same part of the chromosome. There are almost certainly errors in our assembly (the genome is highly repetitive) and in our map (because there is very, very low recombination across most of the chromosome - about 3/4 of the physical map is actually localized at above 60cm).
> > >
> > > Do you have any thoughts about what those dips are? I'm assuming they're picking up on errors in our assembly or map. And should we worry too much about the converging? This is mostly just another way to localize something we already know.
> > >
> > > Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone :)

I’m trying to use the r/qtl2 analysis on the CC mice.
The phenotype is in the line level, but the extra data is in the mouse level (age of tumor development, gender and so on).
Is it possible that the phenotype will be as binary file of the CC lines and the covariates file will be with the data by each mouse?
Another question, I can’t find the gene map and genotype data of all the CC lines that I have, but in the r/qtl I used the condensed file with all the markers in the CC lines, can I use it also in the r/qtl2?

messages.subject: Re: r/qtl2 analysis on the CC mice
messages.subject_clean: r/qtl2 analysis on the CC mice
messages.body_plain:
> The phenotype is in the line level, but the extra data is in the mouse level (age of tumor development, gender and so on).
> Is it possible that the phenotype will be as binary file of the CC lines and the covariates file will be with the data by each mouse?

If you want to control for covariates at the individual level, you're maybe going to have to do something that is more complicated than what R/qtl2 provides, and I think you're going to want to use phenotypes measured at the individual level, too.

> Another question, I can’t find the gene map and genotype data of all the CC lines that I have, but in the r/qtl I used the condensed file with all the markers in the CC lines, can I use it also in the r/qtl2?

If you have data in R/qtl1 format, you can load it into R with qtl::read.cross() and then convert it to R/qtl2 format with qtl2::convert2cross2()
The CC genotypes that I have were taken from Srivastava et al. (2017) and are at https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2data/tree/main/CC

karl
